templates.dsc: A long sentence does the world. The short one that follows does the meaning. Important caveat, measured: this is a DELIBERATE DEVICE, not his default rhythm. Only about 1.6% of his sentences are a 25-word-plus sentence answered by a 6-word one. On average a long sentence is followed by a longer-than-average one. Use the beat to land a judgement, not as a metronome.
templates.demo: He rebuilt the checkout flow three times, tested every variant, and shipped it on a Friday because he could not bear another week of the old one. It changed nothing.

templates.dsc: Introduce an unfamiliar word by dropping a 1-6 word plain-English gloss between commas. No parentheses, no 'which means'. The gloss is grammatically disposable - delete it and the sentence still stands.
templates.demo: She wanted sannidhya, nearness, more than she wanted answers.

templates.sh: abstract claim → physical thing in the room → 4-word verdict
templates.dsc: Never deliver an abstraction twice in a row. State the idea, then point at something already present, then confirm in four words or fewer. The metaphysics is pointed at, not argued.
templates.demo: Ambition is not the problem. He pointed at the treadmill in the corner. "That's the problem."

templates.sh: [number you paid] → [the claim] → [what you are not saying]
templates.dsc: Before a claim strong enough to sound like a lecture, state what it cost you, with a number and zero adjectives. Make the claim. Then bound it. The order is fixed - the limit comes after, never before.
templates.demo: I spent eleven months and ₹4 lakh on ads that did not convert. Positioning beats creative. I am not saying creative does not matter.

templates.sh: problem in 'we' → one crossover → instruction in 'you'
templates.dsc: Every sentence naming a fault goes in first person plural. Every sentence giving an instruction goes in second person. One clean crossover, not an alternating mess. Ranked lists go in third person so nobody has to admit which rung they are on.
templates.demo: We ship the thing we can build instead of the thing they asked for. You can fix that in one afternoon: read the last twenty support tickets before you open the design file.

templates.sh: story ends on a line → repeat that line → colon → principle
templates.dsc: End the anecdote on a line of speech. Open the next paragraph by repeating that exact line, then a colon, then the principle in twelve words or fewer.
templates.demo: "I just wanted someone to tell me it was fine." I just wanted someone to tell me it was fine: reassurance is a product, and almost nobody sells it.

templates.sh: It is not a [wrong object]. It is a [right object].
templates.dsc: Name the wrong mental model your reader is already running, as a physical object, then name the right one. The analogy now does argumentative work rather than decoration.
templates.demo: A landing page is not a brochure. It is a doorway. A brochure is browsed; a doorway is walked through or it is not.

templates.sh: Q? shorter q? shorter q? → answer next sentence
templates.dsc: Three or four questions, each strictly shorter than the last, the later ones beginning lowercase so the stack reads as a single breath. Answer immediately.
templates.demo: What actually makes someone buy on the first visit? the thing they check before price? the one line they need to see? It is proof that somebody like them already did.

templates.dsc: End the most intense passage on a clock reading or a measurement, never on a reflection. The number re-anchors the reader to the physical world at the exact moment the prose could inflate.
templates.demo: I sat there and let it go, all of it, the whole rotten year of it. The clock read 4.12 a.m.

templates.sh: replace every intensifier with a count
templates.dsc: Adjectives are for objects. Numbers are for feelings. Swap 'huge', 'endless', 'countless' for a specific, slightly odd figure. Round numbers read as estimates; odd ones read as records.
templates.demo: Not "we tested loads of headlines." We tested forty-one headlines over nine weeks.

templates.sh: claim → name the three rational explanations → decline to persuade
templates.dsc: Offer the reader their disbelief before they can form it. Name the likely rational counter-explanations yourself. Then explicitly refuse to argue. The refusal is what buys the credibility.
templates.demo: You can put this down to survivorship bias, or a good month, or luck. Any of those could be right. I am not trying to convince you.

templates.sh: claim → image → restate claim in the image's noun
templates.dsc: The beat almost everyone skips. State the point, show the object, then state the point again using the object's own vocabulary. That third beat converts an image into an explanation.
templates.demo: Attention compounds. A groove cut into rock by one thin line of water a day. Your attention is the water; the groove is the only thing you will be remembered for.

templates.dsc: His primary causal hinge in the late books, up thirtyfold since 2014. It hands off from one movement to the next without a transition paragraph.
templates.demo: And so, the page went live with nothing above the fold but a sentence.

templates.sh: object in the scene → 'would' → consequence years later → resumption cue
templates.dsc: Jump forward in time using 'would' as a tense of destiny, not of conditionality. Trigger it off a physical object in the present scene so the leap feels caused rather than authorial, then return immediately.
templates.demo: He kept the first cheque in a drawer. It would sit there for nine years, outlasting two companies and one marriage. "Anyway," he said, sliding the drawer shut.

templates.dsc: His workhorse ending, roughly a third of all chapter closes. Two or three short imperatives, rhythmically balanced. It only works if the body of the piece already used 'you' heavily - then it reads as permission rather than order.
templates.demo: Ship it ugly. Fix it live.

templates.dsc: Close by compressing the piece's central abstraction into a portable definition of ten words or fewer. This is the ending most likely to get quoted back at you.
templates.demo: Taste is just the speed at which you notice something is wrong.

templates.sh: Granted / Then again / Having said that, X. But Y.
templates.dsc: Raise the counter-case against yourself before the reader does, then turn. He does this rather than defending, and it reads as confidence rather than hedging.
templates.demo: Granted, nobody asked for a rewrite. But nobody was reading the old one either.

templates.sh: Truth be told, [admission that costs you]
templates.dsc: A flag that always precedes an admission that lowers you. Used thirteen times in one 2024 book. It buys the right to assert in the next paragraph.
templates.demo: Truth be told, I had not read the brief properly.

patterns.dsc: The single most misread thing about his prose, and I got it wrong first too. Memoir to memoir his mean sentence length went UP, 13.6 to 14.1 words. But the popular fix - follow a long sentence with a short one - is measurably false. Across 91,862 sentences, the sentence after a 30-word-plus sentence averages 17.7 words against a 14.6 mean. Longer. In every one of the 15 books, no exceptions. Long sentences cluster together. What is actually distinctive is the width of his range: he writes both 4-word and 40-word sentences, where most writers live in a narrow middle.
patterns.do: Stop trying to alternate. Widen instead: make sure you actually write some sentences under 8 words and some over 30, and check the spread rather than the sequence. Save the short-after-long beat for the handful of moments that deserve a verdict.

patterns.nm: He did not shorten his words. He swapped which long words.
patterns.dsc: Mean word length did not move at all across a decade. Words of nine characters or more held steady. What collapsed was Latinate abstraction - the -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity layer fell about 35% in his instructional prose. What replaced it: proper nouns, named objects, Sanskrit terms with inline glosses, clock times.
patterns.do: Do not simplify. Substitute. Every abstract noun gets replaced by the named thing it was standing in for.

patterns.nm: He breaks Stephen King's rule, and keeps the half that matters
patterns.dsc: King says the road to hell is paved with adverbs. Tested against 950,000 words, Om Swami splits the rule in two. He does NOT purge -ly adverbs - he runs 10 to 13 per thousand words, which is ordinary for English prose. What he strips is one specific kind. Adverbs of MANNER, the ones that describe how a thing was done, run at just 1.3 per thousand words in his 2024 books, down 31% from his early ones. Roughly one every 750 words. The adverbs he keeps almost all MEASURE instead: completely, exactly, nearly, barely, merely, simply. Simply is his single most-used adverb in every era of both corpora. On King's hardest rule - never modify a dialogue tag - he is near-absolute: 5 instances in a whole 2024 book, and across the late corpus he writes plain 'said' 165 times against 36 uses of every other tag combined.
patterns.do: Do not hunt -ly words. Hunt manner adverbs specifically. If the adverb tells the reader HOW, cut it and fix the verb. If it tells them HOW MUCH or HOW EXACTLY, keep it. And never put one next to said.

patterns.dsc: His biggest compressor. Quoted dialogue is reserved for emotional turns and decisions. Everything logistical - a refusal, an agreement, a plan - gets one line of reported speech. A lesser writer stages both scenes.
patterns.do: Go through your draft. Any exchange conveying procedure becomes one reported sentence. Only exchanges where somebody changes their mind keep their quotation marks.

patterns.nm: Spend your own status, never the reader's.
patterns.dsc: The butt of nearly every joke is the teacher, the expert, the master, or himself. He is the fool in his own anecdotes. Having done that, he can then write an absolute sentence and it reads as observation rather than sermon.
patterns.do: If a joke's target is your reader or your customer, cut it. If your piece has no joke at your own expense, you have not paid for your strongest claim.

patterns.nm: Language magnitude must not track event magnitude.
patterns.dsc: Twenty-two hours of daily meditation for months gets summarised in two words. The most transcendent event in a 52,000-word book is closed with a timestamp. He states in the prologue that he understates everything about himself - and then never compensates for it later.
patterns.do: Find your biggest moment. Cut its adjectives to zero. End it on a measurement.

patterns.nm: Get plainer as the stakes rise.
patterns.dsc: Measured, and counterintuitive. His longest sentences and longest words appear in dry technical exposition. His shortest words appear in the starvation chapter; his shortest sentences at the two visions. Where a normal writer reaches for grandeur, he reaches for monosyllables.
patterns.do: Measure your most emotional passage and your most technical one. If the emotional one has longer words, invert it.

patterns.nm: Delete the paragraph that explains what the scene meant.
patterns.dsc: The clearest difference between his 2014 and 2024 books. Early Om Swami renders a scene, then adds a paragraph telling you its significance. Late Om Swami keeps one sentence of that paragraph and moves it inside the scene. Everything else is deleted.
patterns.do: Find your explaining paragraph. Keep its best sentence. Move that sentence up into the action. Delete the rest.

patterns.nm: Close on an opening, not a resolution.
patterns.dsc: His 2014 chapter endings close a loop and settle. His 2024 endings open one. Four words at the end of a chapter is the cheapest retention gain available in the whole corpus.
patterns.do: Rewrite the last sentence of every section as something unresolved. One sentence of work per section.

patterns.nm: The vehicle is always humbler than the subject.
patterns.dsc: His analogies come from kitchens, tamed animals, small children, weather, and machines you have personally operated. Never aviation, physics, war, or neuroscience. Explaining a high idea with a washing machine is a status transaction: it says the idea is not above you.
patterns.do: Ban any source domain that is more impressive than your subject. Cut every analogy at the end of its second sentence and never call it back.

patterns.dsc: He raises questions and declines to answer them - by deferring to a later chapter, naming competing versions without picking one, asserting that further reasons exist, or simply declaring something unfathomable. The prose reads as knowing more than it says. That is where 'profound' actually comes from.
patterns.do: Raise a real question. Refuse it once, cleanly. If it reads as evasion rather than authority, the surrounding prose did not have enough hard specifics in it.

patterns.dsc: His 2015 books interrupt a chapter on grief with a five-step exercise. His 2024 books batch every procedure into an appendix or a link. Narrative runs clean; method is exiled.
patterns.do: Pull every numbered how-to out of your prose and put it at the end. If the piece collapses without it, the prose was carrying the instruction badly.

patterns.nm: Be most specific exactly where you are least believable.
patterns.dsc: His starvation chapter counts hours. His vision chapter inventories the colour of a garment and then notes that the colour contradicts what he had read. Contradicting your own expected iconography is a credibility instrument - an invented account matches the picture book; a real one does not.
patterns.do: Find your least believable true claim. Add a detail that contradicts what a reader would expect, and say that it does.

neverdo: Semicolons yoking two independent clauses - he cut 83% of them in ten years
A participle before the subject: 'Spotting the cab, I waved' → 'I waved'
The gloss paragraph after a scene, explaining what the scene meant
Latinate register-lifters: ineluctably, cogent, salutary, obversely
Hedge-then-retract: 'I'm not saying X, but at the same time…'
'Studies show' or 'research suggests' - zero across 216,000 words of teaching prose
Adverbs modifying 'said' - 8 in a whole 2024 book
Exclamation marks in your own voice - 5 in 52,000 words, all in dialogue
Extending a metaphor past its second sentence, or calling it back later
Weather or landscape as a chapter opening
'Little did I know', 'words cannot describe', 'a shiver ran' - all zero
Summarising at the close. No 'in conclusion', no key-takeaways box
Jokes at the reader's expense. Sarcasm anywhere
Closing on fear or consequence - every close is permission or promise
